clue.text: See 7
Determined 1 cycling is overtaken by true rogue

indicators.note: to be overtaken by is to be passed and then surrounded, so the jumbled letters enclose the cycled fish
rogue as an adjective means out of control, so the letters of true run wild into a new order
cycling means the letters go round, the last moving to the front

parts.note: 1 is the entry FISH, and a sole is a fish

explanation.surface: A determined fish on a bike is overtaken by a genuine scoundrel.
explanation.walkthrough: In this puzzle a clue number 1 stands for the answer at 1, FISH, so a sole. 'cycling' moves its last letter to the front (ESOL), and 'rogue' rearranges TRUE around that.
explanation.definitionFit: Resolute describes someone firm of purpose, so it is a synonym for determined.

clue.text: Down-and-dirty

definitions.meaning: low in spirits, the mood sense of the colour
smutty — the sense a comedian's material has when it is too near the knuckle

explanation.surface: Getting down-and-dirty: the phrase for wading into something rough and grubby.
explanation.walkthrough: Hyphens make 'Down-and-dirty' read as one idiom, and that is the whole disguise: the two halves are separate definitions with a link word between them. Four letters covering both senses is a very short clue's worth of work.
explanation.definitionFit: Feeling blue is being downcast and a blue joke is a dirty one — two everyday senses of one colour word, neither of them about colour.

clue.text: Metal producers manufactured steel frames occasionally

indicators.note: Something manufactured has been assembled out of parts into a new arrangement, which is what happens to the letters beside it.

parts.note: anagram fodder

indicators.note: Reading a word occasionally means dipping in every so often rather than straight through, so only every second letter is taken.

parts.note: every second letter of fRaMeS

explanation.surface: A fabrication yard that knocks up steel frames now and then.
explanation.walkthrough: Every word belongs to one picture of a metalworking firm, so nothing announces itself as fodder or as instruction. 'Occasionally' is worth banking: it almost always means take every other letter.
explanation.definitionFit: A smelter is the works that draws metal out of ore with heat, so the plural names producers of metal in the plainest sense.

clue.text: Thoroughly investigates tips from The Repair Shop to cover boring item

indicators.note: to cover means the first letters go around the tool
the tips of the words are their first letters, which are taken

parts.note: the opening letters of these three words are used
an awl is a pointed tool for boring holes

explanation.surface: Advice from a TV restoration programme on how to hide a dull object.
explanation.walkthrough: The Repair Shop is a BBC programme in which craftspeople restore heirlooms. 'tips from' takes T, R and S, and 'to cover' wraps them round AWL; 'boring' means drilling, not dull.
explanation.definitionFit: To trawl through something is to search it exhaustively, as a fishing net sweeps the sea.

clue.text: Words in song embracing trouble ending for Crystal Palace

indicators.note: To embrace is to get both arms right round something, so the word doing it closes over the letters named next.

parts.note: the verses are a song's words, as against its tune
to ail somebody is to trouble or afflict them

indicators.note: 'Ending for' asks only for the letter that finishes the word it points at.

parts.note: the last letter of CrystaL

explanation.surface: A songwriter's lyrics taking in the latest misery at Crystal Palace.
explanation.walkthrough: Crystal Palace are a south London football club, so their name reads as one thing and splits into two: 'Crystal' lends its last letter and 'Palace' is the whole definition. A one-word definition beside ten letters usually means most of the clue is wordplay.
explanation.definitionFit: Definition by example: Versailles is one particular royal palace outside Paris, standing in for the general word.

clue.text: Flash Gordon in on the talks with Flash Liquid to produce a novel quote

indicators.note: A liquid holds no shape of its own, so the letters it describes are free to run into any order.

parts.words: Flash Gordon in on the talks with Flash
parts.note: anagram fodder, 28 letters — both Flashes are in it, and 'with' only joins the second one on

explanation.surface: Flash Gordon sits in on the negotiations alongside a bottle of Flash, the kitchen cleaner.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Flash' looks like an instruction both times it appears and is fodder both times; the shuffling is ordered by the innocent-looking 'Liquid'. Douglas Adams gave the line to the dolphins leaving Earth, then used it as the title of his fourth Hitchhiker novel.
explanation.definitionFit: The line is the dolphins' farewell in Douglas Adams's Hitchhiker books and the title of the novel it names, so 'a novel quote' is literal.

clue.text: Strip from page 1

parts.note: p = page, the standard abbreviation
1 down is FISH, and the clue leaves you to pick a species — the long thin one fits

explanation.surface: Tearing a strip off page one of the paper.
explanation.walkthrough: '1' is a cross-reference rather than a numeral: it stands for 1 down's FISH and you choose a species with the right letters. 'Strip' is doing duty as a verb.
explanation.definitionFit: To peel is to strip the skin or covering off something, so the two verbs swap straight into each other.

clue.text: Perfect 1-wood

parts.note: the Roman numeral for one
deal is sawn fir or pine, the plank sort of timber

explanation.surface: A golfer's flawless drive off the tee with the 1-wood.
explanation.walkthrough: '1' has meant a fish everywhere else in this grid, and here it is simply the Roman numeral — the one place the cross-reference does not apply. Deal is softwood timber, the stuff of shelves and floorboards.
explanation.definitionFit: 'Perfect' and IDEAL are the same adjective — nothing left to improve on — and either can replace the other in a sentence.

clue.text: Communication system is common kind for Spooner

indicators.note: Dr Spooner was famous for swapping the starting sounds of words, so the opening sounds of the two words change places

parts.note: common means coarse, vulgar
a mode is a kind or manner

explanation.surface: A statement that something is a common type, as the Reverend Spooner would put it.
explanation.walkthrough: COARSE MODE with its first sounds swapped is spoken as 'morse code'; the swap works on sound, since COARSE is said like CORSE.
explanation.definitionFit: Morse code is the telegraph system of dots and dashes for sending messages, a means of communication.

clue.text: Wales played by captain's physical principle

indicators.note: by means alongside, so the captain's name sits beside the jumbled letters

parts.note: Captain Hook is the pirate in Peter Pan; the 's stands for 'is', linking to the definition

indicators.note: played means performed in a new arrangement, so the letters are rearranged

explanation.surface: A rugby or football report: Wales are up against the opposing captain.
explanation.walkthrough: Captain Hook is the villain of Peter Pan; 'captain's' gives HOOK, with the 's working as 'is'. 'played' rearranges WALES to ESLAW, which goes 'by' HOOK.
explanation.definitionFit: Hooke's law states that a spring's extension is proportional to the force on it, a law of physics.

clue.text: Hotel entertained by country backing group

indicators.note: to be entertained by someone is to be a guest inside their home, so the letter goes inside
backing means going backwards, so the country's name is read in reverse

parts.note: Laos is a country in South-East Asia
Hotel is H in the NATO phonetic alphabet

explanation.surface: A hotel hosts a group of country music backing singers.
explanation.walkthrough: 'backing' reverses LAOS to SOAL, and 'entertained by' puts H inside it after the S.
explanation.definitionFit: A shoal is a large group of fish swimming together, so the answer is a collective noun meaning a group.

clue.text: Sweet Caroline's opening fight in Madison Square Garden

indicators.note: the opening of a word is its first letter

parts.note: the name Caroline, whose first letter is taken
a rumble is American slang for a fight, and Madison Square Garden is the famous New York boxing venue

explanation.surface: 'Sweet Caroline' is sung as a fight gets under way at a New York arena.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Sweet Caroline' is the Neil Diamond song sung at sports events, but 'Sweet' is the definition. Madison Square Garden places the fight in America, where a rumble means a brawl.
explanation.definitionFit: Crumble is a baked pudding of fruit under a crumbly topping, and in Britain a sweet is a dessert.

clue.text: Allure of 1 million

parts.note: 1 down again asks for a fish; a char is the trout's cousin from cold northern lakes
m = million, the standard abbreviation

explanation.surface: The allure of a cool million in the bank.
explanation.walkthrough: '1 million' reads as a single quantity, which is the trap — the 1 breaks off as the cross-reference and the million is one letter. Once you know the theme, every '1' is a fish waiting to be named.
explanation.definitionFit: Charm is the pull a person exerts on other people, which is what 'Allure' means — the same noun in the same countable sense.

clue.text: Spanish players delivered part of song

parts.note: Barça is what everyone calls FC Barcelona
ROLLED, as a bowler delivers a ball, without its last letter

explanation.surface: Barcelona's players giving a snatch of a song before kick-off.
explanation.walkthrough: Barça for Barcelona is a name setters reach for whenever a clue mentions Spanish players. A barcarolle is the swaying boat song of the Venetian gondoliers; Offenbach wrote the famous one.
explanation.definitionFit: 'Song' sits one level above the answer, which is a particular kind of song — a gondolier's, in the rocking rhythm of the oars.

clue.text: Heather in Shropshire borders close to the heart of Percy Thrower

indicators.note: close to means right next to, so the middle letter follows
in means the heather goes inside the border letters
the borders of a word are its first and last letters

parts.note: the county name, of which only the outer letters are used
ling is another name for heather

indicators.note: the heart of a word is its middle letter

parts.note: the name Percy, of which only the centre letter is taken

explanation.surface: Heather grows on the Shropshire border near a gardener's heart, a nod to TV gardener Percy Thrower.
explanation.walkthrough: Percy Thrower was a famous British TV gardener, so 'Thrower' looks like part of his name; it is the definition. Shropshire is an English county on the Welsh border.
explanation.definitionFit: A slinger is someone who hurls stones with a sling, so the word means one who throws.

clue.text: Amber perhaps originally yellowish-red

parts.note: Amber Rudd is a British politician, and 'perhaps' flags her as one example of the surname

indicators.note: What a word is originally is what it starts as, so only its opening letter is wanted.

parts.note: the first letter of Yellowish

explanation.surface: A stone of amber described as having started out a yellowish-red.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Yellowish-red' looks like one colour and is two jobs: the Y is borrowed off the front and only the second half defines. A rudd is also a fish, which is no accident in this grid.
explanation.definitionFit: Ruddy is the adjective for a healthy red colour, most often of a face, so 'red' is the plain sense with the definition hiding at the end of a compound.

clue.text: Agree Machiavelli partly reflected The Prince

indicators.note: Taking words partly means using a run of them as they stand and leaving the rest alone.
A reflection shows you the same thing the other way round, so the run of letters is read backwards.

parts.note: a run of five letters straddles the gap between these two words, starting partway into the first

explanation.surface: Someone half agreeing with Machiavelli's handbook on how princes should behave.
explanation.walkthrough: The italics make The Prince look like the book, which is where the definition hides in plain sight. An ameer — emir in the commoner spelling — is a Muslim prince or commander.
explanation.definitionFit: An ameer is a prince or ruler in the Arab world, the same title as emir, so the definition is straight while pretending to be a book title.

clue.text: 1 main partner

parts.note: the main is an old poetic word for the open ocean, kept alive by the Spanish Main
a partner in marriage

explanation.surface: The number-one partner in a person's life.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Main' looks like an adjective attached to 'partner' and is a noun in its own right, the open sea. The seawife is a wrasse, so 1 down's cross-reference does the defining on its own.
explanation.definitionFit: '1' points at 1 down's FISH, and this one is a species of wrasse — the definition names the family and leaves you to find the member.

clue.text: Potted game eaten by Bill

indicators.note: Whatever is eaten ends up inside the eater, so these letters go within the ones named next.

parts.note: a bill is a poster or advertisement — hence the two letters, as in billboard
bridge is the card game

explanation.surface: Bill tucking into potted game at the table.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Potted game' is lunch on the surface and neither word means what it looks like: 'potted' is the definition, in the sense of a potted history, and the game is played with cards.
explanation.definitionFit: A potted account is a shortened one, and abridged is what a publisher calls a text cut down — the same adjective from a different trade.

clue.text: Fat detective wearing hat

indicators.note: You wear a hat by putting your head inside it, so the wearer's letters go within the hat's.

parts.note: lid is slang for a hat
PI = private investigator

explanation.surface: A portly sleuth in a hat.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Fat' opens the clue looking like an adjective describing the detective, and it is the noun definition. Lid for hat and PI for private eye are two of the shortest cuts in the setter's kit.
explanation.definitionFit: A lipid is the biochemist's name for the family of molecules that fats belong to, so 'Fat' is the kitchen word for the same substance.

clue.text: 1 brief period gripping nation

indicators.note: To grip something is to close your hand right round it, so these letters wrap the piece named next.

parts.note: PHASE, a period of time, shorn of its last letter
the nation dropped into the gap

explanation.surface: A short spell of unrest taking hold of a whole country.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Brief' belongs to the surface's picture of a short political crisis and is really an instruction to dock a letter. The definition is the bare '1', pointing back at 1 down, and the plural comes from the enumeration.
explanation.definitionFit: '1' means 1 down's FISH, and piranhas are South American river fish, so the definition names the family and the wordplay picks the member.

clue.text: Harry Lime drinking tea for 1?

definitions.note: a forename for FISH, the answer at 1: Michael Fish was a BBC weatherman

indicators.note: drinking means taking something in, so the tea goes inside
to harry is to harass or disturb, so the letters of Lime are disturbed into a new order

parts.note: cha (char) is British slang for tea

explanation.surface: Harry Lime, the villain of The Third Man, sips tea.
explanation.walkthrough: Harry Lime is the Third Man villain, but 'Harry' here is the verb to harass. Michael Fish was a famous BBC TV weather forecaster, so the answer is a first name for 1 (FISH).
explanation.definitionFit: Michael Fish is the well-known British weatherman, so Michael is the forename that goes before Fish.

clue.text: Group of hot men in bed

indicators.note: 'In' is the container instruction: everything before it is placed inside the word that follows.

parts.note: a cot is a bed
H is the letter on the hot tap
OR = Other Ranks, the British Army's term for everyone below officer

explanation.surface: Feverish soldiers laid up in bed.
explanation.walkthrough: OR for men is British Army shorthand — Other Ranks — and setters use it constantly. A cohort was originally a tenth of a Roman legion, so the soldiers on the surface are quietly on the answer's side.
explanation.definitionFit: A cohort is a body of people banded together, originally a Roman infantry unit and now any set treated as one, so 'Group' is a plain synonym.

clue.text: Shed Seven essentially leaving the Eastern Mediterranean with nothing

indicators.note: What leaves is gone, so the letter named is taken out of the word it was sitting in.
The essence of a word is the letter at its very centre, with equal numbers either side.

parts.note: the Levant is the region along the eastern Mediterranean coast
the middle letter of seVen, and it is this that goes
O is nothing, the shape of a zero

explanation.surface: Shed Seven quitting the eastern Mediterranean with nothing to show for the tour.
explanation.walkthrough: Shed Seven are a York britpop band, so their name opens the clue as one unit — but 'Shed' alone is the definition and 'Seven' is wordplay. Splitting a proper name across the two halves is Brockwell's favourite move.
explanation.definitionFit: A lean-to is a shed with a single sloping roof propped against a wall, so 'Shed' names it by its commonest kind.

clue.text: Shivering après-skier may finally put new coat on

indicators.note: shivering means shaking, so the letters are shaken into a new order
finally takes the last letter of each of the two words before it

parts.note: the words skier and may, whose last letters are used

explanation.surface: After a day on the slopes, a cold skier might want another layer.
explanation.walkthrough: Après-ski is the socialising after skiing. 'finally' takes R from SKIER and Y from MAY, and 'Shivering' rearranges them with APRES.
explanation.definitionFit: To respray something, such as a car, is to give it a fresh coat of paint.

clue.text: Ashe regularly missed out in Court No.1

definitions.note: number 1 in this puzzle is FISH, and the wahoo is a fish

indicators.note: in means the letters go inside the word for court

parts.note: to woo someone is to court them

indicators.note: every other letter is missed out, so alternate letters are kept

parts.note: the name Ashe, of which alternate letters are taken

explanation.surface: Arthur Ashe, the tennis champion, keeps missing his shots on the show court at Wimbledon.
explanation.walkthrough: Arthur Ashe was an American tennis champion, and Court No.1 is a Wimbledon show court; here 'Court' is the verb woo. 'regularly missed out' keeps A and H of ASHE, which go 'in' WOO.
explanation.definitionFit: The wahoo is a fast game fish of warm seas, so it is an example of FISH, the puzzle's number 1 answer.

clue.text: See 18 Across
See 7 Down
Pikachu's sandwich contains dog meat

indicators.note: What something contains is already sitting inside it, so the letters are there in order and untouched.

parts.note: four consecutive letters straddle the join between these two words, apostrophe and all

explanation.surface: Pikachu's packed lunch turning out to have dog in it.
explanation.walkthrough: Hidden runs are hardest to spot across a word break, and this one crosses an apostrophe as well. Huss is what a fishmonger calls dogfish — rock salmon on a chip-shop menu.
explanation.definitionFit: Huss is the trade name for dogfish flesh, so 'dog meat' is literal rather than jokey: the dog in question is a small shark.

clue.text: Clairvoyant brought up on drugs

indicators.note: In a down clue, bringing something up carries it back towards the top of the grid, so its letters are read upwards.

parts.note: re = on, as in a memo headed 'on the subject of'
E is ecstasy, and the clue's plural asks for more than one of them

explanation.surface: A fortune-teller who was raised on narcotics.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Brought up' is positional, not biographical: in a down clue it lifts the assembled letters back up the grid. 'On' for RE is the memo-heading sense, and Es have meant ecstasy tablets since the 1990s.
explanation.definitionFit: A seer is one who sees — a person with sight of what others cannot see — which is what a clairvoyant is, noun for noun.

clue.text: See 7 Down
Flat 1 has entrance in Shepherd's Bush?

indicators.note: The entrance is the way in, so it wants the letter you go in by — the first one of the word it points at.

parts.note: the first letter of Shepherd’s
Kate Bush, the English singer of Wuthering Heights

explanation.surface: A ground-floor flat whose front door opens onto Shepherd's Bush.
explanation.walkthrough: Shepherd's Bush is a district of west London and reads as a single address, which is the trap: the two words separate, and the Bush is Kate. 'Flat' belongs to the definition, not to the estate agent.
explanation.definitionFit: 'Flat 1' asks for a flat member of 1 down's FISH, and a skate is the broad diamond-shaped ray sold on the fishmonger's slab.
